title: The Final Days
year: Safar to Rabi'ul-Awwal 11 AH — May to June 632 CE
era: The Curtain He Raised at Fajr
teaser: He spent his last days settling debts, freeing slaves, and offering his own back to anyone he had wronged.

layers.title: The Setting
layers.subtitle: Habits changed before anyone read them
layers.content:
The signs were in his practice before they were in his body, and al-Mubarakpuri gathers them.

In Ramadan of the tenth year he withdrew into the mosque for twenty days instead of the ten he had kept every year before. That year the angel Jibreel went through the Qur'an with him twice rather than once. At Arafat he had said he did not know whether he would meet them in that place again. Surat An-Nasr came down at Mina, and he understood it as notice of a departure.

In the early days of Safar of the eleventh year he rode out to Uhud and prayed over the martyrs there, which looked like a man saying goodbye to the dead and the living in one visit. Then he climbed the pulpit and told the people: I am to precede you and I have been made witness upon you. By Allah, you will meet me at the Hawd very soon. I have been given the keys of the treasures of the earth. By Allah, I do not fear for you a return to polytheism after me, but I do fear that you will compete with each other over worldly riches. One night at midnight he went out to the graveyard at al-Baqi' and asked forgiveness for those buried there, and said to them: we are also coming to you.

None of this looked like an ending from the outside. In that same month of Safar he was assembling a large army under Usamah bin Zaid to ride against the Byzantine frontier.

Then, on Monday the twenty-ninth of Safar, he attended a burial at al-Baqi'. On the way home he developed a headache, and his temperature climbed so high that the heat could be felt through the cloth covering his head.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari — the address from the pulpit before his illness, and the visit to the martyrs of Uhud
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: Five Days Before
layers.subtitle: Seven waterskins, then he asked to be repaid
layers.content:
He was ill for thirteen days, or fourteen — the reports differ. For eleven of them he still led the prayers himself.

As the sickness deepened he began asking his wives the same question: where shall I stay tomorrow? Where shall I stay? They understood what he was asking and told him to stay wherever he wished. He was brought to Aishah's room leaning on al-Fadl bin al-Abbas and Ali bin Abi Talib, his head banded, his feet dragging on the ground. He spent his last week there, while Aishah recited al-Mu'awwidhat over him, blew on her hands, and passed them over his body.

On Wednesday, five days before the end, the fever spiked and he fainted. When he came round he said: pour out on me seven waterskins of water, so that I may go out and speak to the people. They seated him in a container and poured until he said, that is enough, that is enough.

He went into the mosque with his head wrapped and sat on the pulpit. He began with a warning about himself. The curse of Allah, he said, falls upon those who made their Prophets' graves places of worship. Do not make my grave a worshipped idol.

Then he opened his own account to the public. He whose back I have ever lashed, he said, I offer him my back so that he may avenge himself on me. He whose honour I have ever insulted, here I am offering my honour so that he may avenge himself. A man stood and said: you owe me three dirhams. He said: Fadl, pay him the money.

He came down, prayed Dhuhr, went back up and resumed. He told them to be good to the Ansar: they are my family and with them I found shelter. Their numbers would shrink, he said, until they were among men as salt is in food. Whoever holds power over people should acknowledge what these men did and overlook their faults.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari — the sermon from the pulpit five days before his death, and the admonition concerning the Ansar
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Turning Point
layers.subtitle: A paper never written, and a man moved forward
layers.content:
Still on the pulpit, he told them a story with no names in it. Allah has given a servant of His the choice between what he desires of this world and what He keeps for him in the next, and the servant has chosen the next.

Abu Bakr started crying and said: may our fathers and mothers be ransomed for your sake. Only later did the rest of the room work out that the servant was the Prophet ﷺ and that Abu Bakr had understood it first. Then he said: if I were to take any Khalil other than Allah, I would have chosen Abu Bakr. No gate shall be kept open into the mosque except his.

On Thursday, four days before the end, in severe pain, he said: come here, I will have you write something through which you will never fall into error. Umar bin al-Khattab said the Prophet was in acute pain and the Book of Allah was with them and was enough. Others wanted it written. He listened to them argue over him, then told them to go away and leave him alone. Nothing was written. Three instructions from that day survive: expel the Jews, Christians and polytheists from Arabia, honour delegations as they had been used to, and a third the narrator forgot.

That evening he could not reach the mosque. Three times water was poured for him, three times he tried to stand, three times he fainted. He sent word: let Abu Bakr lead the prayer. Aishah asked three or four times that her father be excused, because he wept too easily to get through it. He refused each time. Abu Bakr led seventeen prayers in his lifetime.

On Saturday or Sunday he came out leaning on two men. Abu Bakr began to withdraw; he gestured him to stay, said seat me next to him, and was placed on his left. He led, and Abu Bakr raised his voice at every takbir so the rows could hear.

On Sunday he freed his slaves, gave away the seven dinars he owned, and handed his weapons to the Muslims. That night Aishah borrowed oil from a neighbour for her lamp. His coat of armour was in pledge to a Jew of Madinah for thirty measures of barley.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari — the choice given to a servant, the refusal to write, and Abu Bakr leading the prayers
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Revelation
layers.subtitle: No verse came down; one had been waiting
layers.content:
On Monday morning the Muslims were praying Fajr behind Abu Bakr when the curtain of Aishah's room lifted. He was looking at them, standing in proper rows, and he smiled. Abu Bakr began stepping back to let him through. Anas bin Malik said the men were so glad they were almost taken out of their prayer. He gestured to them to carry on, went back inside, and drew the curtain. He was not alive for the next prayer.

During the day he whispered something to Fatimah that made her cry, then something else that made her laugh. She explained afterwards: first that he would not recover, then that she would be the first of his family to follow him. He asked for al-Hasan and al-Husain, kissed them, and asked that they be looked after. He called his wives in and told them to remember Allah. He told Aishah he could still feel the food he had tasted at Khaybar, and that it felt as if death were approaching.

At the end Aishah held him against herself. Her brother came in with a siwak; he looked at it, and she understood, took it, softened it in her own mouth and gave it to him, and he used it as well as he could. There was a water pot within reach. He put his hand in it and wiped his face and said: there is no God but Allah. Death is full of agonies. Then he raised his hand toward the ceiling and she heard him say: with the Prophets and the truthful and the martyrs and the good doers. O Allah, forgive me and have mercy on me and join me to the most exalted Companionship on high. He said the last words three times. Then his hand came down.

It was late morning, Monday the twelfth of Rabi'ul-Awwal, 11 AH. He was sixty-three years and four days old.

No revelation is recorded as having come down during the illness. The Qur'an had been closed at Arafat. What settled the hour after his death was a verse years old, and Abu Bakr found it.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari — the last Fajr seen from the curtain, Fatimah's weeping and laughing, and his death in Aishah's room
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: What It Left Behind
layers.subtitle: A verse, an argument, and a grave under a bed
layers.content:
Madinah heard within the hour. Anas said he had never known a brighter day than the one the Prophet ﷺ arrived among them, nor a darker one than the day he died.

Umar would not accept it. The hypocrites, he told the people, were claiming the Messenger of Allah had died; he had gone to his Lord as Moses did for forty nights, and would come back.

Abu Bakr rode in from as-Sunh, went into Aishah's room, uncovered his face, kissed him and wept: Allah will not cause you to die twice; you have experienced the death He ordained. Then he came out, told Umar to sit, and when he would not, addressed the crowd instead.

He who worships Muhammad should know that Muhammad is dead. But he who worships Allah — He is Ever Living and He never dies. Then he recited: «وَمَا مُحَمَّدٌ إِلَّا رَسُولٌ قَدْ خَلَتْ مِن قَبْلِهِ الرُّسُلُ» — 'Muhammad is no more than a Messenger, and indeed many Messengers have passed away before him.' (3:144) The verse sits in the Uhud passage of Surat Al-Imran, where a rumour of his death had once broken the Muslim ranks.

Ibn Abbas said it was as though nobody had heard the verse until Abu Bakr recited it, and then everyone was. Umar said his legs gave way under him, and only then did he understand.

While his body lay covered on the bed, the succession was settled in the roofed passage of Bani Sa'idah. He was washed on Tuesday with his clothes on and shrouded in three white Yemeni sheets. Abu Bakr said he had heard him say a Prophet is buried where he dies, so Abu Talhah lifted the bed he had died on and dug beneath it. People came in ten at a time to pray over him, each praying alone with nobody leading. Aishah said they only knew he was being buried when they heard digging tools in the depth of the night.

Carry this. He left no palace, no treasury, no written appointment, and an armour in pawn for barley. What he left was a book, a congregation that knew who should stand in front of it, and a verse telling them he was never what they worshipped.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari — Abu Bakr's address and the recitation of 3:144; the washing and burial
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

quiz.prompt: How long was the Prophet ﷺ ill before he died?

options.text: Three days
Thirteen or fourteen days — the reports differ
A full lunar month
Forty days, matching the forty nights of Moses

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — The Start of the Disease
quiz.scholar_reflection: The sources agree the illness began on Monday the twenty-ninth of Safar and ended on Monday the twelfth of Rabi'ul-Awwal, and they agree he led the prayers himself for eleven of those days. The total count is given as thirteen or fourteen.

quiz.prompt: From the pulpit five days before his death, what did he offer the people?

options.text: A share of the treasury of Madinah
The name of the man who would succeed him
His own back and his own honour, so that anyone he had injured could take revenge
Release from their oath of allegiance to him

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — Five Days Before His Death
quiz.scholar_reflection: One man in the crowd took him up on it, for three dirhams, and was paid on the spot. That is the entire recorded balance of twenty-three years of authority over that city.

quiz.prompt: On the Thursday he asked for writing materials so he could dictate something that would keep them from error. What was written?

options.text: A document naming Abu Bakr as his successor
Nothing — the people argued about whether he should dictate, and he sent them away
A charter dividing Arabia between his commanders
His will, distributing his property among his daughters

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, cited in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — Four Days Before His Death
quiz.scholar_reflection: Umar said the Book of Allah was with them and was enough; others wanted the dictation taken. He heard them dispute over him and told them to leave him. Nothing was written down.

quiz.prompt: What was the condition of his property on the Sunday before he died?

options.text: It was placed in trust for his grandsons
He divided it equally among his nine wives
He freed his slaves, gave away his seven dinars and his weapons, and his armour was in pledge for thirty measures of barley
It had been consumed by the mobilisation of Usamah's army

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — A Day Before His Death
quiz.scholar_reflection: That same night Aishah borrowed lamp oil from a neighbour. He had ruled the whole of Arabia and his household could not light a lamp on its own credit.

quiz.prompt: Which verse did Abu Bakr recite to the crowd after his death, and where does it sit in the Qur'an?

options.text: 'This day I have perfected your religion for you' (5:3), from the Farewell Pilgrimage
'When the help of Allah comes, and the victory' (110:1), revealed at Mina
'Muhammad is no more than a Messenger' (3:144), in the passage of Al-Imran about Uhud
'Indeed you are to die, and indeed they are to die' (39:30), from Surat az-Zumar

quiz.citation: Quran 3:144, recited by Abu Bakr as reported in Sahih al-Bukhari and cited in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: Ibn Abbas said it was as though nobody had ever heard the verse before Abu Bakr recited it, and then everyone was reciting it. It had been in the Qur'an since the years after Uhud.

quiz.prompt: He asked for materials to write something that would keep them from error, was argued over, and let it go. What do you make of the fact that nothing was written?

options.text: What was needed already existed — the Book and the Sunnah
It is a genuine loss, and the argument caused it
He could have insisted and did not, which tells me something
I cannot settle it, and I would rather not pretend to

quiz.slider_label: Nothing was lost — Something was lost
quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari — Four Days Before His Death, cited in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Sealed Nectar reports the episode without resolving it, and lists the three instructions of that day with the honest note that the narrator forgot the third. Muslims have read this scene differently for fourteen centuries.

quiz.prompt: He never named a successor in words. He did move Abu Bakr to the front of the prayer and refuse to move him back. Which of those is the clearer instruction?

options.text: The action — where a man stands at prayer says everything in that community
Neither; leading a prayer is not the same as governing a state
He deliberately left it to them, and they decided at Bani Sa'idah
Silence was the instruction — no dynasty, no appointment

quiz.slider_label: He indicated clearly — He left it open
quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari — Abu Bakr leading the prayers during the final illness
quiz.scholar_reflection: Aishah asked three or four times to have her father excused, because he wept too easily to get through it. He refused every time. Abu Bakr led seventeen prayers while the Prophet ﷺ was still alive.

quiz.prompt: His first words from the pulpit that week were a warning not to turn his own grave into a place of worship. Why start there?

options.text: He knew exactly how grief turns a man into an object of worship
It protects the one thing everything else rests on — that only Allah is worshipped
It is a strange priority for a dying man, and that is the point
He was speaking about earlier communities more than about his own

quiz.slider_label: Guarding his memory — Guarding the tawhid
quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, and Muatta' Imam Malik — 'Do not make my grave a worshipped idol'
quiz.scholar_reflection: Days later Abu Bakr said the same thing in different words to a crowd that had lost its bearings: he who worships Muhammad should know that Muhammad is dead. The warning and the reminder are the same sentence twice.

quiz.prompt: Umar refused to believe he had died and threatened anyone who said it. Abu Bakr kissed his face, wept, and then recited a verse. Which response do you recognise in yourself?

options.text: Umar's — refusal is the first thing grief does
Abu Bakr's — I reach for something solid and stand on it
Neither; I go quiet and functional and feel it later
Both, in that order, and the second takes longer to arrive

quiz.slider_label: Deny it first — Name it first
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — Umar's Attitude and Abu Bakr's Attitude
quiz.scholar_reflection: Umar is not criticised in the account. He said his legs collapsed under him when the verse was recited, and only then did he understand. The sources let the strongest man in Madinah be the one who could not take it in.

quiz.prompt: The funeral prayer was performed in groups of ten, each person praying individually with nobody leading. What does that arrangement say?

options.text: No one was going to stand in front of him, even then
It was practical — the room was small and the city was large
It made every mourner's farewell individual rather than collective
It quietly avoided a fight over who had the right to lead it

quiz.slider_label: A practical measure — A statement of rank
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — Preparations to His Honorable Body
quiz.scholar_reflection: It took all of Tuesday and most of Wednesday, ten at a time, in the order of his clan, then the Emigrants, then the Helpers, then the women, then the children. He was buried at night, under the bed he had died on.
